opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I was looking for someone who had already been where I wanted to go. At that point I was mostly teaching myself. I was reading papers, implementing things, and trying to figure out what actually mattered in reinforcement learning and game theory. But when you're self-taught, you don't really know what you don't know. You can spend months on something a more experienced researcher would tell you in five minutes is a dead end.

Johannes had done work I really admired. His work on combining deep learning with game-theoretic methods for imperfect-information games was right at the intersection I cared about. So it wasn't just "this person is smart and at a famous lab." It was that he had thought deeply about exactly the problems I was obsessed with.

I think what I was really after was taste. Anyone can learn the math eventually, and you can learn to write the code. What's hard to learn on your own is judgment: which problems are worth working on, which experiments will actually tell you something, and when an idea is promising versus just complicated. Having someone who could look at what I was doing and say "this part is interesting, this part isn't" was incredibly valuable.

And frankly, I also wanted someone who would take me seriously even though I didn't have the usual credentials. I wasn't coming through a PhD program. Finding a mentor who cared about the ideas and the work, rather than where you came from, mattered a lot to me.

r001.rationale: The response values Johannes’s judgment and feedback, and suggests it could save time, but does not describe seeking recurring criticism as a way to learn how to conduct research.

r002.rationale: The response does not say Eric wanted to outperform an algorithm Johannes had developed during his PhD.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time I was a teenager teaching myself machine learning from papers and YouTube lectures, and I had hit the point where I could implement things, but I had no idea whether what I was doing was actually good. There's a big gap between being able to reproduce a result and knowing what questions are worth asking. I didn't have a university, I didn't have a lab, I didn't have anyone around me who had done research at a high level.

So what I was really looking for was taste. Johannes had come out of David Silver's group, he'd worked on reinforcement learning at DeepMind, and I wanted someone who could look at an idea and tell me within a few minutes whether it was interesting or whether I was fooling myself. That kind of feedback loop is incredibly hard to get on your own. You can spend months going down a path that an experienced researcher would have dismissed in an afternoon.

The other thing was just calibration. When you're working alone, you either overestimate yourself or you lose confidence completely, and you swing between the two. Having someone who knew what the frontier actually looked like, who could say, this part is genuinely novel and this part has been done, that grounded me. And I think I was also quite direct about it. I basically cold-emailed him, told him what I was working on in poker and imperfect information games, and asked if he'd be willing to talk. I expected nothing, and he said yes. A lot of my career has come from asking people things I thought they'd say no to.

r001.rationale: He says he wanted Johannes’s feedback on which research ideas were worthwhile and describes that feedback as a loop that could save months of pursuing weak directions.

r002.rationale: He mentions working on poker and imperfect-information games, but does not say he asked Johannes for help outperforming an algorithm Johannes developed during his PhD.
